How a turn works

When the agent acts, the compiler gets a veto.

For consequential work, the model writes Jo against the capabilities you grant — and Jo has to type-check before anything happens.

STEP 1

You send a message

A turn begins. The agent's standing instructions and memory come along for context.

STEP 2

The model writes Jo

It can answer directly. To act, it authors a small runTask program describing the work for this turn.

STEP 3

jo compiles it

Against the granted capabilities. Reference one you don't have and compilation fails — right there.

STEP 4

It runs — or it doesn't

A program that compiled runs. One that didn't never executed a line. The gate is the checkpoint.

The receives list is the agent's entire authority — and it's re-proven on every single turn, not signed off once in review.
// what this agent may touch receives stdout // print
receives booking // reserve seats
receives payment // ✗ not granted
receives files, net, shell … // ✗

What you get

A framework, three agents, and no hidden runtime.

Capabilities, proven every turn

Authority is a typed receives list, checked by the compiler each turn — not a policy file that drifts from the code.

Bring any model

Anthropic or OpenAI, provider-agnostic behind one Model interface. Swap with an env var.

Three agents, ready to run

Terminal, browser, and Telegram drivers ship in the box. Copy one, edit its identity, done.

Skills & memory

Read-only reference the agent consults on demand, plus a durable scratchpad it curates itself.

Just a Jo project

Run it with jo run. No bespoke runtime, no framework magic — the toolchain you already have.

Defense in depth

The compile gate decides authority; an external OS sandbox confines the process. Two independent walls.
